poster.text: The enterprising investor looks for a discount along three tracks. Track one: undervalued stable companies - profitable, but out of favor; wait for the rotation. Track two: secondary companies - mid-sized, unknown, with cash and a business but without analyst coverage; the lack of attention IS the margin. Track three: special situations - mergers, liquidations, restructurings where the outcome can be calculated from public documents. And the tool that made Graham legendary: net-nets - companies whose market capitalization is below net current capital (current assets minus ALL liabilities). In practice you buy the company for less than its cash. Net-nets are rare today in the large universe - but the principle is eternal: there is a price at which even an average company is a gift.

poster.text: Margin of safety is the bridge built for 30 tons when the trucks weigh 10. If you buy at 30-50% below conservatively calculated value you have room to be WRONG - if the business deteriorates, if the analysis contains mistakes, if the business cycle turns. Without a margin you must be RIGHT not to lose; with a margin you can be wrong and survive. This is the difference between hope and calculation. The margin comes in three forms: a price matched against value (assets or earning power), diversification (you never know which position will fail) and a demand for predictability (the more uncertain the future, the greater the margin). The whole history of investing in one sentence: never accept a price at which you must be right.
